author: "Simon Frost"

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using MatrixCommunityModels
using LinearAlgebra, Printf, Random, Statistics
using Plots
```

## Park's beetles

Thomas Park grew two flour beetles, *Tribolium confusum* and *T. castaneum*, together in
vials of flour for twenty years, and one species nearly always died out. The results became
a textbook case of competitive exclusion. One culture of Leslie, Park & Mertz (1968) did
not fit: the two species lived together for 960 days. Edmunds et al. (2003) suggested that
the culture was on a stable cycle on which both species persist, alongside two stable
states in which one of them is lost. Desharnais et al. (2005) explored the same model with
other parameters and with demographic noise.

In flour beetles the competition is cannibalism and predation. Larvae and adults eat eggs,
and adults eat pupae, of their own species and of the other. The model is the
larva-pupa-adult (LPA) model of Dennis et al. (1995) for each species, with a time step of
two weeks, coupled through what each eats of the other.

## One beetle

For one species,

$$L_{t+1} = b A_t \exp(-c_{el} L_t - c_{ea} A_t), \qquad P_{t+1} = (1 - \mu_l) L_t, \qquad
A_{t+1} = P_t \exp(-c_{pa} A_t) + (1 - \mu_a) A_t,$$

where `L` are feeding larvae, `P` non-feeding larvae, pupae and callow adults, and `A`
adults. The exponentials are the shares of eggs and pupae that escape being eaten. In the
two-species model of Edmunds et al. (2003) the exponents gain the larvae and adults of the
other species, each with its own rate.

The printed two-species adult equations of Edmunds et al. (2003) read `... − (1 − µa)aₜ`,
with a minus sign, in both species and in the typeset PDF, not only in extracted text. Read literally, adults that survive would be subtracted. The single-species
equation on the same page, and the two-species equations of Desharnais et al. (2005), add
them. The sign here is a plus, and the checks below against the numbers that Desharnais et
al. print hold only with a plus.

Each species is a net with four transitions. `flour_beetle` builds it:

```{julia}
beetle = flour_beetle(:castaneum; b = 10, mu_l = 0.2, mu_a = 0.02,
                      eats = [:castaneum => (larvae_eggs = 0.025, adults_eggs = 0.025, adults_pupae = 0.03)])
transition_names(system(beetle)[:castaneum])
```

Recruitment of larvae and emergence of adults are multiplied by `exp(-pool)` for two pools
named after the species, `castaneum_eggs` and `castaneum_pupae`. Each beetle adds to those
pools, its own and the other species', the rate at which its larvae and adults eat eggs
and its adults eat pupae. Composing two beetles gives four pools, one per victim stage and
species:

```{julia}
beetles = flour_beetle_competition(TRIBOLIUM_EDMUNDS_2003)
pool_names(beetles)
```

## The model of Desharnais et al. (2005)

Desharnais et al. list every parameter (their Table 1) and print several states of the
model that can be checked. Species 1 is *T. castaneum* and species 2 *T. confusum*;
`c_el[i, j]` is the rate at which larvae of species `j` eat eggs of species `i`.

```{julia}
d05 = flour_beetle_competition(TRIBOLIUM_DESHARNAIS_2005)
vertical = periodic_point(d05, [0, 0, 0, 100.0, 100, 100], nothing)
horizontal = periodic_point(d05, [98.0, 78, 40, 0, 0, 0], nothing)
twocycle = periodic_point(d05, [9.0, 247, 45, 0, 0, 0], nothing; period = 2)
show2(v) = join([@sprintf("%.2f", x) for x in v], ", ")
println("species 2 alone:      (", show2(vertical.n[4:6]), ")")
println("species 1 alone:      (", show2(horizontal.n[1:3]), ")")
showeig(λs) = join([@sprintf("%.5f", real(l)) * (abs(imag(l)) > 0 ? @sprintf(" ± %.5fi", abs(imag(l))) : "")
                  for l in unique(x -> (round(real(x); digits = 8), round(abs(imag(x)); digits = 8)), sort(λs; by = real))], ", ")
println("  its eigenvalues:    ", showeig(horizontal.multipliers))
println("  at (98.36, 78.69, 40.93): ", showeig(eigvals(jacobian(d05, [98.36, 78.69, 40.93, 0, 0, 0], nothing))))
println("species 1 two-cycle:  (", show2(twocycle.n[1:3]), ") and (", show2(advance(d05, twocycle.n, nothing)[1:3]), ")")
```

The paper gives (0, 0, 0, 114.04, 91.23, 148.14) for *T. confusum* alone, an unstable
equilibrium (98.36, 78.69, 40.93, 0, 0, 0) of *T. castaneum* alone with eigenvalues −1.1219,
−0.1586, −0.0026 ± 0.06754i, 0.86528 and 0.59352, and a two-cycle of *T. castaneum* alone
through (9.36, 247.55, 45.48) and (309.43, 7.49, 52.59). The states agree to the digits
printed. The eigenvalues at the exact equilibrium differ from the printed ones in the
fourth decimal place; at the equilibrium rounded as printed they agree to every digit, so
the paper's Jacobian was evaluated at the rounded point. Its invasion criterion for *T. castaneum* at the *T. confusum*
equilibrium is

```{julia}
p = TRIBOLIUM_DESHARNAIS_2005
L2, A2 = vertical.n[4], vertical.n[6]
round(p.b[1] * (1 - p.mu_l[1]) / p.mu_a[1] * exp(-p.c_el[1, 2] * L2 - (p.c_ea[1, 2] + p.c_pa[1, 2]) * A2); digits = 2)
```

as printed (0.29 < 1: the equilibrium resists invasion, whatever `c_el[2, 1]`).

The paper varies `c_el[2, 1]`, the rate at which *T. castaneum* larvae eat *T. confusum*
eggs. From Park's starting point, four adults of each species, it reports a coexistence
two-cycle for 0.092 < `c_el[2, 1]` < 0.17, an invariant loop (a "double loop") for 0.061 to
0.092, and only the *T. confusum* equilibrium below 0.061:

```{julia}
with21(c) = flour_beetle_competition(merge(TRIBOLIUM_DESHARNAIS_2005, (c_el = [0.012 0.01; c 0.003],)))
steps(com, n, k) = (for _ in 1:k; n = advance(com, n, nothing); end; n)
for c in (0.05, 0.07, 0.10, 0.15)
    com = with21(c)
    x = steps(com, [0, 0, 4.0, 0, 0, 4], 5000)
    e = periodic_point(com, x, nothing; period = 2)
    on_cycle = e.converged && maximum(abs.(e.n .- x)) < 1e-6 && maximum(abs.(e.multipliers)) < 1
    println(@sprintf("c_el[2,1] = %.2f: ", c),
            sum(x[1:3]) < 1e-6 ? "T. castaneum lost" : on_cycle ? "stable coexistence two-cycle" : "coexistence, not on a cycle")
end
```

```{julia}
loop = with21(0.062)
x = steps(loop, [0, 0, 4.0, 0, 0, 4], 2000)
orbit = reduce(hcat, accumulate((n, _) -> advance(loop, n, nothing), 1:3000; init = x))
scatter(orbit[3, :], orbit[6, :]; ms = 1, msw = 0, label = "", xlabel = "T. castaneum adults",
        ylabel = "T. confusum adults", title = "c_el[2,1] = 0.062")
```

At `c_el[2, 1] = 0.062` the adults of the two species circle a closed curve with two loops,
the double loop of Desharnais et al.'s Fig. 2.

Desharnais et al. also give a stochastic version: larvae are Poisson, and survival from
stage to stage is binomial. That is the demographic stochasticity of `project` with an
`rng`, since recruitment is marked as births and every other transition is a survival
probability. At `c_el[2, 1] = 0.062`, starting from four adults of each species, they
report that after 150 steps both species persist in 30% of runs, *T. castaneum* is lost in
15% and *T. confusum* in 55%:

```{julia}
ens = ensemble(loop, [0, 0, 4.0, 0, 0, 4], fill(nothing, 150); replicates = 2000, rng = Xoshiro(2005))
lost1 = abundance(ens, :castaneum)[:, end] .== 0
lost2 = abundance(ens, :confusum)[:, end] .== 0
(both_persist = mean(.!lost1 .& .!lost2), castaneum_lost = mean(lost1), confusum_lost = mean(lost2))
```

## The bifurcations of Edmunds et al. (2003)

Edmunds et al. take *T. confusum* as species 1 and *T. castaneum* as species 2, in 8 g of
flour (`V = 0.4` of their 20 g unit). They set `b = 10`, `µl = 0.2`, `µa = 0.02`, every
egg-eating rate to 0.01, and the rates of eating pupae to `cpa = 0.01` and `cPA = 0.012`
(within species), `cPa = 0.005` and `cpA = 0.008` (between). They then raise the two rates
at which larvae eat the other species' eggs together, `ceL = cEl = c`, from 0.016 to 0.032,
and find five regions (their Fig. 2):

- A: a stable coexistence equilibrium that every start reaches;
- B: *T. castaneum* always wins;
- C: a stable coexistence equilibrium alongside the *T. castaneum* state;
- D: whichever species has the advantage wins, as in Lotka-Volterra competition;
- E: both exclusion states and a stable coexistence two-cycle.

Each species alone has an equilibrium that does not depend on `c`:

```{julia}
P = TRIBOLIUM_EDMUNDS_2003
pair(c) = flour_beetle_competition(merge(P, (c_el = [0.01 c; c 0.01],)))
confusum_alone = periodic_point(pair(0.02), [30.0, 30, 100, 0, 0, 0], nothing).n
castaneum_alone = periodic_point(pair(0.02), [0, 0, 0, 30.0, 30, 100], nothing).n
(confusum = round(sum(confusum_alone); digits = 1), castaneum = round(sum(castaneum_alone); digits = 1))
```

Both near 160 animals, the level of the axis states in their Fig. 2 (whose vertical axes
count all three stages). The boundaries between the regions are found here by bisection:
where each species' equilibrium becomes stable against invasion by the other, where a
stable coexistence equilibrium appears beside the *T. confusum* state, and where a stable
coexistence two-cycle appears.

```{julia}
stable(x) = maximum(abs.(x.multipliers)) < 1
resists(c, alone) = stable(periodic_point(pair(c), alone, nothing))
function coexistence_equilibrium(c)      # reached from T. confusum alone with a few T. castaneum adults
    com = pair(c)
    x = steps(com, confusum_alone .+ [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.5], 20000)
    min(sum(x[1:3]), sum(x[4:6])) < 1e-3 && return false
    e = periodic_point(com, x, nothing)
    e.converged && all(>(0), e.n) && stable(e)
end
function coexistence_cycle(c)            # reached from 16 adults of each species
    com = pair(c)
    x = steps(com, [0, 0, 16.0, 0, 0, 16], 20000)
    min(sum(x[1:3]), sum(x[4:6])) < 1e-3 && return false
    e = periodic_point(com, x, nothing; period = 2)
    e.converged && all(>(0), e.n) && stable(e) && maximum(abs.(advance(com, e.n, nothing) .- e.n)) > 1e-6
end
function boundary(test, lo, hi; tol = 1e-5)
    below = test(lo)
    while hi - lo > tol
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        test(mid) == below ? (lo = mid) : (hi = mid)
    end
    return round((lo + hi) / 2; digits = 4)
end
edges = (AB = boundary(c -> resists(c, castaneum_alone), 0.016, 0.024),
         BC = boundary(coexistence_equilibrium, 0.021, 0.0245),
         CD = boundary(c -> resists(c, confusum_alone), 0.022, 0.03),
         DE = boundary(coexistence_cycle, 0.026, 0.031))
```

Read from their Fig. 2, the boundaries are at 0.0200, about 0.0243, about 0.0252 and about
0.0288. The diagram can be drawn by following each branch of equilibria and two-cycles with
Newton's method (`periodic_point`), starting from a known point and stepping `c`:

```{julia}
function branch(cs, guess; period = 1)
    out = NamedTuple[]
    for c in cs
        e = periodic_point(pair(c), guess, nothing; period)
        (e.converged && all(>(1e-6), e.n)) || break
        push!(out, (c = c, n = e.n, next = advance(pair(c), e.n, nothing), stable = stable(e)))
        guess = e.n
    end
    return out
end
A = branch(0.016:0.0002:0.024, [8.0, 6, 34, 21, 17, 69])
C = branch(0.0248:-0.00002:0.024, steps(pair(0.0248), confusum_alone .+ [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.5], 20000))
C2 = branch(0.0248:0.00002:0.0256, C[1].n)
saddle = branch(0.032:-0.0002:0.023, [17.0, 14, 51, 13, 10, 42])
two = branch(0.032:-0.0001:0.028, [0.62, 16.68, 40.14, 3.05, 32.19, 67.78]; period = 2)

function diagram(k, name)
    total(n) = k == 1 ? sum(n[1:3]) : sum(n[4:6])
    plt = plot(; xlabel = "c = ceL = cEl", ylabel = name, legend = false, ylims = (-5, 180))
    alone = k == 1 ? confusum_alone : castaneum_alone
    switch = k == 1 ? edges.CD : edges.AB
    plot!(plt, [0.016, switch], fill(sum(alone), 2); ls = :dash, color = :black)
    plot!(plt, [switch, 0.032], fill(sum(alone), 2); color = :black, lw = 2)
    plot!(plt, [0.016, 0.032], [0, 0]; color = :gray)
    for b in (A, sort(vcat(C, C2); by = x -> x.c), saddle)
        isempty(b) && continue
        for s in (true, false)
            pts = [x for x in b if x.stable == s]
            isempty(pts) || scatter!(plt, [x.c for x in pts], [total(x.n) for x in pts];
                                     ms = s ? 2.5 : 1.5, msw = 0, color = s ? :black : :gray)
        end
    end
    scatter!(plt, [x.c for x in two], [total(x.n) for x in two]; ms = 2.5, msw = 0, color = :firebrick)
    scatter!(plt, [x.c for x in two], [total(x.next) for x in two]; ms = 2.5, msw = 0, color = :firebrick)
    vline!(plt, collect(edges); color = :gray, ls = :dot)
    return plt
end
plot(diagram(2, "T. castaneum (all stages)"), diagram(1, "T. confusum (all stages)"); layout = (2, 1), size = (700, 700))
```

Black points are stable equilibria with both species, grey points unstable ones, red points
the two values of the stable two-cycle, and the horizontal lines each species alone (solid
where it resists invasion). The unstable two-cycles of the paper's figure are not followed.
The picture is that of Edmunds et al.: the coexistence equilibrium of region A meets the
*T. castaneum* state at the A-B boundary; a stable and an unstable coexistence equilibrium
appear together at the B-C boundary, and the stable one meets the *T. confusum* state at the
C-D boundary; the unstable one, a saddle, runs on through D and E; and a stable two-cycle
appears at the D-E boundary. At `c = 0.016` the coexistence equilibrium has

```{julia}
(confusum = round(sum(A[1].n[1:3]); digits = 1), castaneum = round(sum(A[1].n[4:6]); digits = 1))
```

animals of each species, against about 58 and 95 read from the figure.

One detail is not in the figure. For a short stretch of region A, where a few points are
grey, the coexistence equilibrium is weakly unstable: its leading multiplier passes
through −1 and back, and a two-cycle of very small amplitude takes its place (a
period-doubling "bubble"):

```{julia}
lead(c, guess) = (e = periodic_point(pair(c), guess, nothing); (e.n, e.multipliers[argmax(abs.(e.multipliers))]))
unstable(c) = abs(lead(c, A[findmin(x -> abs(x.c - c), A)[2]].n)[2]) > 1
bubble = (from = boundary(unstable, 0.018, 0.0186), to = boundary(unstable, 0.0188, 0.0196))
eq, m = lead(0.0186, A[findmin(x -> abs(x.c - 0.0186), A)[2]].n)
x = steps(pair(0.0186), eq .+ 0.01, 50000)
(; bubble..., multiplier_at_0186 = round(m; digits = 5),
 adults_on_the_cycle = (round.(x[[3, 6]]; digits = 2), round.(advance(pair(0.0186), x, nothing)[[3, 6]]; digits = 2)))
```

The two adult numbers of the cycle differ by a fraction of an animal, so at the scale of the
published figure the equilibrium and the cycle cannot be told apart.

## Region E: coexisting on a cycle

On the two-cycle the life stages of the two species rise and fall together, as Edmunds et
al. point out: larvae of both are many in one step and few in the next.

```{julia}
cyc = two[1]
(c = cyc.c, larvae_step1 = round.(cyc.n[[1, 4]]; digits = 2), larvae_step2 = round.(cyc.next[[1, 4]]; digits = 2),
 adults_step1 = round.(cyc.n[[3, 6]]; digits = 1), adults_step2 = round.(cyc.next[[3, 6]]; digits = 1))
```

Which outcome a culture reaches depends on where it starts. Leslie et al. started their
cultures with adults only; here every pair of adult numbers from 2 to 128 is projected for
5000 steps (about 190 years):

```{julia}
counts = 2.0 .^ (1:7)
function outcomes(c)
    com = pair(c)
    [begin
         x = steps(com, [0, 0, a1, 0, 0, a2], 5000)
         sum(x[4:6]) < 1e-3 ? 1 : sum(x[1:3]) < 1e-3 ? 2 : 3
     end for a2 in counts, a1 in counts]
end
basins = [outcomes(c) for c in (0.028, 0.032)]
plots = [heatmap(string.(Int.(counts)), string.(Int.(counts)), b; c = cgrad([:steelblue, :darkorange, :firebrick], 3; categorical = true),
                 clims = (1, 3), colorbar = false, xlabel = "T. confusum adults at the start", ylabel = "T. castaneum adults at the start",
                 title = "c = $c") for (b, c) in zip(basins, (0.028, 0.032))]
plot(plots...; layout = (1, 2), size = (800, 360))
```

Blue: *T. confusum* wins; orange: *T. castaneum* wins; red: both persist (on the two-cycle).
At `c = 0.028` (region D) *T. castaneum* wins unless *T. confusum* starts with several
times as many adults; at `c = 0.032` (region E) a band of starts between the two, in which
*T. confusum* has one to four times as many adults, leads to coexistence. The coexistence culture started with 32
*T. confusum* and 4 *T. castaneum* adults:

```{julia}
[c => (x = steps(pair(c), [0, 0, 32.0, 0, 0, 4], 20000); sum(x[4:6]) < 1e-3 ? "T. castaneum lost" : "both persist")
 for c in (0.028, 0.030, 0.032)]
```

In the deterministic model that start lies in the basin of *T. confusum* alone, in both
regions D and E. Edmunds et al. place the culture in region E in their Fig. 3 and show a
stochastic run with `c = 0.031` from that start in which the species coexist (their Fig. 4);
their argument is that the culture moved from region D into region E during the
experiment, and that noise acts on the trajectory. The deterministic model alone does not
take that start to the cycle.

## What is measured and what is assumed

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Model: LPA for each species, coupled by eating eggs and pupae | | Edmunds et al. 2003; Desharnais et al. 2005 |
| 2003: habitat `V`; `b`; `µl`; `µa` | 0.4; 10; 0.2; 0.02 | Edmunds et al. 2003, rounded from estimates for *T. castaneum* (Dennis et al. 2001) |
| 2003: egg-eating rates within species, and between species by adults | 0.01 | Edmunds et al. 2003 |
| 2003: pupa-eating rates `cpa`, `cPA`, `cPa`, `cpA` | 0.01, 0.012, 0.005, 0.008 | Edmunds et al. 2003, chosen, not fitted |
| 2003: egg-eating between species by larvae `ceL = cEl` | varied, 0.016 to 0.032 | Edmunds et al. 2003 |
| 2005: all 18 parameters | Table 1 | Desharnais et al. 2005, from statistical fits and assays |
| Sign of surviving adults in the two-species adult equation | plus | the 2003 print has minus; plus as in its single-species model and in the 2005 paper |

Neither paper fits the model to Park's data, which count adults only; Edmunds et al. call
their values "biologically reasonable". The data of Leslie et al. (1968) and Park et al.
(1964) are in those papers and were not used.

What agrees and what does not:

- Every state and criterion printed by Desharnais et al. (2005) is reproduced to the digits
  printed, and so are its eigenvalues when, as it seems they were, they are computed at the
  equilibrium rounded as printed (at the exact equilibrium they differ by up to 1.2e-4); and so are the shares of stochastic outcomes they give at
  `c_el[2, 1] = 0.062` (to within the sampling error of 2000 runs).
- The four boundaries of Edmunds et al. (2003) are reproduced to within the precision
  with which they can be read from their figure, and so are the levels of the axis states,
  the region A equilibrium, the saddle and the stable two-cycle.
- Within region A the coexistence equilibrium gives way, over a short stretch of `c`, to a
  two-cycle so small that the figure could not show it; the paper does not mention it.
- The 2003 adult equation is printed with a minus sign; with it the published checks fail
  and adults would be removed by surviving. It is taken to be a typesetting error.
- From the coexistence culture's own start (32 and 4 adults), the deterministic model goes
  to *T. confusum* alone at every `c` tried, though the paper's Fig. 3 places that culture in
  region E. The paper's own argument rests on noise and on a change in the strains, so this
  need not contradict it, but it is not shown here.

Both papers were read in full: the 2003 paper as text extracted from its PDF, with the
equations and Fig. 2 checked on the rendered pages, and the 2005 paper likewise, with its
Table 1 read from the rendered page. Dennis et al. (1995, 2001), Leslie et al. (1968) and
Park et al. (1964) were not read. Neither paper has published code; nothing was digitised
from their figures except the region boundaries and levels read by eye for comparison.
